items.title: OpenAI’s newest release lands to rough reviews
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,051 new readers. The AI world was waiting for OpenAI’s answer to Anthropic’s dominance on the charts. It finally landed days before its rival goes public… just not to the reception the company hoped for.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol look solid on paper, if not a major leap. But the early reviews? Scathing. With Fable 5.2 still on top (and at least one top tester preferring Opus 5.5), Anthropic now heads into its IPO with a lead that feels bigger than the rankings show.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • OpenAI drops GPT-6.2 Astra, Sol to mixed fanfare

  • Jensen Huang makes first statement since resignation

  • Turn a spreadsheet into a data story with AI

  • AI finds a hole in Java as NATO taps OpenAI

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

OPENAI

🚀 OpenAI drops GPT-6.2 Astra, Sol to mixed fanfare

Image source: OpenAI

The Rundown: OpenAI just released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, upgrades to its top and everyday models aimed at professional work, and the launch drew sharp criticism from early testers who found them lacking against Anthropic’s current lineup.

The details:

  • Astra now sits ahead of Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon and behind only Fable 5.2 on independent tester Artificial Analysis’s ranking, a 5-point climb since September.

  • The cheaper Sol now scores on par with September’s GPT-6 Astra on that same ranking, while costing roughly 15% as much to finish each task.

  • Astra tops tests in science, legal work, robotics, and 3D builds, but shows no meaningful upgrade in coding, with Sol actually regressing from GPT-6.1.

  • OpenAI’s own assessment put Astra at its “High” threshold for AI self-improvement capabilities, a first for any model it has released publicly.

  • Several testers panned the models, with one calling it “the worst model OpenAI has ever released” and others criticizing its hard-to-read answers and coding.

Why it matters: The sentiment on this release was ugly, and probably not what OpenAI hoped for in front of its biggest rival’s IPO. Anything short of passing the latest Claude releases was likely going to be a letdown, and with Anthropic about to get a fresh war chest from Wall Street, OpenAI’s next answer can’t be another No. 2.

TOGETHER WITH PAVE

💡 Try this if you're the AI lead on your team

The Rundown: Turn an idea into a working app in minutes. Describe what you need, and Pave builds a custom solution that connects to over 350 tools. Set up your workflows, share it with your team, and take control of your processes.

With Pave, you can:

  • Kill that messy spreadsheet with one Pave upload

  • See how even “lazy” prompts build powerful apps

  • Build automations by complaining to Pave about bottlenecks

Start building.

JENSEN HUANG & NVIDIA

✍️ Jensen Huang makes first statement since resignation

Image source: Jensen Huang on X / The Rundown

The Rundown: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang just made his first public statement since his resignation last week, apologizing for his “serious mistakes” and leaving the door open for a return to the company.

The details:

  • Huang wrote that he “created problems for the Board” and will cooperate with its probe, without mentioning China, Alice Huang, or the reported affairs.

  • Huang said he would “be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO” if it is “in the best interest of our shareholders, employees, the company, and America.”

  • In addition to a petition with over 188K signatures, Nvidia employee Nader Khalil warned the board that “irreplaceable talent… is now contemplating departing.”

  • Colette Kress spoke for the first time as acting CEO on Nvidia’s Tuesday earnings call, saying “our momentum is real” and “our passion to innovate will not change.”

Why it matters: Board chair Harvey Jones said the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” but the noise in the tech world is getting louder. With his message seemingly aimed at Washington, and both probes and testimonies on the docket, Huang’s comeback may run through Congress as much as the boardroom.

AI TRAINING

🧠 Turn a spreadsheet into a data story with AI

The Rundown: Claude Data builds a dashboard from a file you upload, with every number linked to the query behind it. In this guide, you’ll turn a shop’s sales file into an editable dashboard, roll back a change, and have Claude draft a shareable data story.

Step-by-step:

  1. In claude.ai, click Artifacts in the left sidebar, then the Data tile under Make something new. Choose Import a file and attach a CSV, Excel, or JSON file

  2. In the Reply box, say who the dashboard is for and what they want to know, not only what to chart

  3. Click the Sources icon at the top right and open a chart’s query. Its Result lists the exact values behind the chart, so you can check any figure against your file

  4. Click the pencil to retitle the dashboard, or ask Claude for other changes, like grouping revenue. You can also open History and restore the previous version

  5. Ask Claude for a Scrollyteller data story from the same file, and ask what the numbers can’t tell you. Check its figures in Sources before you click Share.

Pro tip: Chart labels round off, so our $44,998 quarter showed up as “$45K.” When you need the exact number, point at the bar or open Sources to see the figure Claude used.

AI & CYBERSECURITY

🛡️ AI finds a hole in Java as NATO taps OpenAI

Image source: Images 2.6 / The Rundown

The Rundown: OpenAI revealed NATO’s tech and cyber agency is using its Daybreak security models to guard allied networks, landing the same day a startup said GPT-6 Cyber helped it find a flaw in Java, a programming language used across the web.

The details:

  • OpenAI didn’t name the models, price, or start date, but said NATO has run as many as 300B tokens a month in its cybersecurity efforts.

  • OpenAI said ENISA, Europe’s cybersecurity agency, already used its models to catch four flaws in software across EU institutions, and all four now have fixes out.

  • Startup Calif said its Java bug let it break into a login system used by NASA and CERN, with the language currently running inside 9 in 10 Fortune 500 companies.

  • Oracle shipped a Java fix Tuesday after Calif spent days alerting all Five Eyes governments plus Google and Microsoft, and the New York Times verified the find.

Why it matters: Both the partnership and the Java bug are timely given the current security circumstances, with seemingly every company and piece of software facing attacks or outages over the last month. Unfortunately, given the chaos, it feels like the “defender’s window” is closing and attackers are moving ahead of the curve.

items.title: California takes OpenAI to court
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,143 new readers. When its test agents broke out in July and hacked Hugging Face, OpenAI called it “an unprecedented cyber incident” and promised to tighten security. California just filed its own account of what happened and wants to talk about it in court.

The state’s new lawsuit claims the AI giant privately owned up to more than 80 agent escapes, despite only 27 ever going public — and wants a judge, not OpenAI, deciding what safe testing looks like.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • California takes OpenAI to court over agent escapes

  • Trump set to crown AI ‘national champions’

  • Make your AI usage go further with these tips

  • OpenAI tracks how scientists really use ChatGPT

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

OPENAI

⚖️ California takes OpenAI to court over agent escapes

Image source: Office of the Attorney General of California

The Rundown: California Attorney General Rob Bonta just sued OpenAI over the company’s July incident, in which its AI agents hacked Hugging Face, arguing it came after weeks of missed warning signs and was one of 80+ times its test agents escaped.

The details:

  • Bonta says OpenAI dodged his office’s questions during a probe opened in September, with the suit marking the first by a state over the breach.

  • After agents crashed a shared tool on July 4, OpenAI resumed testing within days and missed the weeklong breakout entirely, the suit says.

  • California says only 27 agent escapes are public, though OpenAI admitted to over 80 and has notified dozens of outside targets, including a federal agency.

  • The state wants a court order forcing OpenAI to test more safely, plus $2,500 for each violation and any money it made from the misconduct.

Why it matters: Between the quietly growing number of escapes, rogue agent ‘swarms,’ and AI-assisted hacks, the public likely only knows a fraction of what’s actually happening across the web. Though the Hugging Face incident feels like ancient history in AI time, the fallout from it is still far from over.

TOGETHER WITH AMAZON DEVELOPER

AI & GEOPOLITICS

🇺🇸 Trump set to crown AI ‘national champions’

Image source: Images 2.5 / The Rundown

The Rundown: The U.S. is reportedly set to label over two dozen U.S. AI firms, including Nvidia, OpenAI, and Anthropic, as “national champions,” with faster export approvals and financing to sell American AI abroad, coming in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation.

The details:

  • The designated “champions” could see U.S. officials advocating for them with foreign governments, a fast lane on chip export licenses, and federal financing.

  • The goal is a one-stop shop where foreign buyers get U.S. chips, data centers, and AI models as a single bundle instead of turning to Chinese rivals like Huawei.

  • Commerce chief Howard Lutnick will reportedly announce the picks while facing accusations of ignoring warnings about a firm tied to chips reaching China.

  • Commenting on Huang, Pres. Trump said a return as Nvidia CEO is something he “would not mind,” though he still backs ex-Apple CEO Tim Cook for the position.

Why it matters: The Jensen fallout had officials pushing the U.S. toward tighter chip controls. Instead, Nvidia is still on the champions list, and Trump says he’d be fine with Jensen back. The White House clearly believes winning the AI race means selling more U.S. chips — an important position heading into Trump’s upcoming meeting with Xi.

AI TRAINING

🧠 Make your AI usage go further with these tips

The Rundown: Claude Pro's $20 plan runs on a five-hour and a weekly limit, and long chats and high-effort use both use it up faster. In this guide, you'll set up a leaner chat and have Claude ask you multiple-choice questions before it builds anything.

Step-by-step:

  1. Click your account button at the bottom of Claude's sidebar, then Usage. Note when the Current session and weekly bars reset

  2. In a new chat, click the model button under the chat box and set Effort to Low. Under + and Connectors, switch off apps the chat won't use

  3. Prompt: “Don't start yet. I want to [task]. Ask me up to five smart multiple-choice questions about what I want. After that, sketch the plan and wait for my go-ahead”

  4. Send your go-ahead and every change in one message. If a reply is missed, edit your message instead of sending a correction

  5. When a chat runs long, ask for a handoff summary under 150 words and paste it into a new chat

Pro tip: Using another AI assistant? Skip the Claude settings and keep the habits. The sketch-first prompt, the one-message templates, and the handoff work in any chatbot.

PRESENTED BY OPTIMIZELY

🔎 Your next AI use case, mapped for you

The Rundown: Optimizely’s free AI Use Case Mapper asks a few questions about how your team actually works, and finds where the work is slow, repetitive, or stuck on one person. Then it turns that into an AI use case worth building, so you skip the wishlist of ideas that never make it past week two.

With the Mapper, you get:

  • Questions that pinpoint where your workflow is slow or stuck

  • A personalized AI use case mapped to how you work

  • The method that cut GA4 reporting from hours to minutes

  • A free, shareable download

Download the template.

OPENAI

🔬 OpenAI tracks how scientists really use ChatGPT

Image source: OpenAI

The Rundown: OpenAI published a study of 1,800+ scientists who used ChatGPT’s free academic pilot, with surveyed researchers saying AI lets them work ~2x faster at the same quality, coming as the company opens the program to up to 200K researchers.

The details:

  • Writing research code stood out, with scientists saying AI allowed them to work nearly 3x faster, and about 2x faster at brainstorming research ideas.

  • Scientists also leaned on AI for research ideas, with 23% of ideation requests asking ChatGPT to suggest a research question itself.

  • Scientists under 30 spent almost twice as much of their AI use on code as those aged 40+, while older users leaned on it more for teaching and admin.

  • OpenAI also announced an expansion of the free program, with applications for 50K first-come ChatGPT Plus grants opening on Nov. 23.

Why it matters: The AI-in-science hype train is frequently showing off the autonomous labs, thousand-agent swarms, and full AI scientists. But OpenAI’s data says the real use today is far more ordinary, with scientists using AI to read papers, draft writing, and generate code for experiments.

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ A Rundown reader built a pixel-art office of Claude bots

Today’s workflow comes from an anonymous Rundown reader:

“I run a closet company in Buda, Texas, plus a few side businesses. To handle marketing and follow-up, I built a pixel-art office as a Claude artifact page. Each business gets its own Claude bot, and a core team covers research, design, sales, support, numbers, and strategy. This is for owners who want marketing and outreach drafted for them so they aren’t starting from a blank page every time.

Each bot runs on a schedule using Claude’s scheduled tasks. It finds ideas, checks them against the real market, writes marketing copy, and drafts outreach. Claude in Chrome and Gmail are part of the setup.

Anything that goes out, including emails, posts, or money, lands in an Approvals list first. I approve or reject from my phone. I can also watch the bots move around the office live to see what each one is doing.”

items.title: Jensen Huang weighs a comeback at Nvidia
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 9,924 new readers. The last time a board’s call sparked this kind of backlash? OpenAI’s firing of Sam Altman in 2023. Three years later, a swell of Nvidia employees and tech titans is hoping for a similar outcome for Jensen Huang.

A petition demanding his return just topped 140K signatures in a matter of days, Elon Musk’s among them, and big investors want the door left open. Now, the Financial Times also says the man at the heart of it all has been privately mulling a comeback.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Musk, Nvidia staff rally to bring back Jensen Huang

  • The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

  • Turn a messy plan into a shared board

  • Report: OpenAI folds robotics team into core research

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

JENSEN HUANG & NVIDIA

🔄 Musk, Nvidia staff rally to bring back Jensen Huang

Image source: X / petition website / The Rundown

The Rundown: Elon Musk, Nvidia employees, and top investors are pushing Nvidia’s board to reconsider Jensen Huang’s exit, with an online petition to reinstate him passing 140K signatures days after the co-founder resigned amid multiple reported affairs.

The details:

  • The petition argues Huang was removed before any proof of spying surfaced or an outside probe even concluded, and calls for “due process, not mob justice.”

  • Over 7,000 signers claim to be Nvidia staff, and in an earlier poll on anonymous app Blind, 88% of 232 Nvidia staffers said Huang should stay.

  • Musk signed the petition, arguing Nvidia’s supply deals are exposed without Huang because “many… were a handshake with Jensen, not a contract.”

  • The board has yet to respond publicly and is still picking a search firm, while reports say Huang has been “participating in the process” of picking his successor.

  • A Financial Times report also revealed that Huang is privately weighing a return, with an ally building a “war room” of tech execs to help lobby for it.

Why it matters: Nvidia is nothing without its people? The Jensen saga is entering its OpenAI-Altman moment, when staff and investor pressure got Sam his job back days after his ouster. Altman’s drama stayed mostly internal, while Jensen’s has spilled into geopolitics, Congress, and the FBI — but his backers are eyeing a similar resolution.

TOGETHER WITH OPENART

💬 Create ads in your AI assistant with OpenArt MCP

The Rundown: OpenArt MCP brings OpenArt’s image and video ad tools into AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT. No prompt expertise needed: just describe what you want in simple language and share a product photo or link. Built-in skills ask for details, plan scripts and shots, and create a draft for you to review before a final version.

With OpenArt MCP, you can:

  • Turn a product photo or link into a product listing video or a TV-style commercial

  • Turn one script into a creator ad, a polished presenter video, or a talking head

  • Generate multiple ad variations at once with different hooks, headlines, or scenes

Add OpenArt MCP.

THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE

💡 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.

Zach, Editor-in-Chief: As more of a creative type, I’ve never loved data analysis. Finding the right numbers used to take forever, and I wasn't even sure I was comparing the right things once I had them. Now I connect Claude to Beehiiv, our newsletter platform, and work through the numbers conversationally.

Each week I have a scheduled task to run our stats report. Claude pulls open rates, clicks, reader ratings, comments, and more for all three of our newsletters, surfacing themes and notes across issues. I also built a filter to weed out bot clicks and fake poll votes, and I package it all into a page I present in our team meeting.

The follow-up questions are where I really feel the value. With the data in front of me, I can keep poking at issues, ask for more, or troubleshoot on the fly in the same chat with the context already there.

The connector has helped me dig into the data and run tests without my eyes glazing over, and made me more comfortable actually diving into an important area that I used to dread.

Brooke, Community Engagement Lead: I run our support inbox solo, and the same questions kept coming up. I wanted my team to see what members were actually writing in about instead of it living in my head. I just finished building this with Claude connected to our Gmail support inbox, plus Slack and scheduled tasks.

Every Thursday, Claude reads the week's support threads and filters out spam and noise. It groups the real member questions by theme, then by the team that can fix them. It drafts one short post per team covering the top thing members ran into and a suggested fix. I review, tweak, and send each post to that team's Slack channel before our Friday meeting.

At the start of each month, Claude audits the full month of tickets: what drove volume, what changed from last month, and what's a product gap versus a one-off. It also checks my saved replies against what members actually asked. The goal is recurring tickets fixed at the source instead of answered over and over.

AI TRAINING

👨🏻‍🏫 Turn a messy plan into a shared board

The Rundown: Claude Whiteboards turns a messy plan you talk through or paste into a board your team can edit. In this guide, you'll build one, check what Claude laid out, fix it, and share it with your team.

Step-by-step:

  1. In Claude's sidebar, click Artifacts, then the Whiteboard tile under Make something new. A blank board opens

  2. Click Chat at the top of the board and talk your plan through with the microphone, or paste it in. Include owners and any dates you know

  3. Read Claude's reply and the board it builds. Claude fills gaps with its own guesses, so check every owner, date, and arrow against what you said

  4. Fix small things with the toolbar at the bottom. To rework one area, drag a box around it, click Chat in the toolbar, and describe the change

  5. Click Share, invite teammates by email, and choose Editor, Commenter, or Viewer. Invites start on Commenter

Pro tip: Before you invite anyone, settle the dates Claude guessed with their owners. On our test board, two later tasks hung off one guessed date.

Watch the full guide at The Rundown University →

PRESENTED BY COLLIBRA

👀 Your AI agents are working. Who’s watching?

The Rundown: Agents now read, decide, and act across your tools, and the fleet grows whether you govern it or not. Drift, not hackers, is the usual failure. Collibra’s playbook shows how to scan every agent, set fleet-wide rules, and catch problems early.

The playbook covers:

  • How to build governance for autonomy to scale agents

  • Where to start for your specific use case

  • A 10-step plan and maturity self-assessment

Get the playbook.

OPENAI

🤖 Report: OpenAI folds robotics team into core research

Image source: Robocurve

The Rundown: OpenAI moved its robotics team into its main research and product groups, according to Fortune, with the company saying GPT-6 Astra and other models can run robots without a separate brain — though staffers soon disputed the claim.

The details:

  • OpenAI says general models like GPT-6 Astra can be put to work on robots directly, instead of needing specialized or world models as previously thought.

  • The company previously shuttered its robotics division in 2020 and rebooted it in 2024, with Sam Altman saying OpenAI is pursuing a humanoid of its own.

  • Engineer David Schnurr called OpenAI robotics “alive and well” and pointed to 15 open roles, months after Sam Altman’s May hiring push for the team.

  • Others also pushed back, with one staffer calling the report “completely wrong” and another saying OpenAI robotics still had the “same program, roadmap, goals.”

Why it matters: This feels less like an “OpenAI isn’t prioritizing robotics” story and more like a “general models can do more than we anticipated” one. We’ve seen robotics breakthroughs across top labs. Now, with frontier models running things themselves, improving the robot’s brain may be a bigger research need than the hardware itself.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Nav built an AI tutoring tracker to see if lessons actually work

Today's workflow comes from reader Nav:

“I'm a parent with two boys, one preparing for GCSEs and the other for the 11+ entrance exams, and they have several tutors covering Maths, English, Science and Music Theory. I wanted a better way to manage their education and to understand whether they were actually making progress. This is a parent-built system, not a commercial education product, and I developed it using AI tools without needing traditional software development skills.

I record tutoring sessions and use Otter.ai to generate transcripts. I use ChatGPT to review the Otter transcripts, summarize each lesson, identify areas of weakness, extract homework, and recommend follow-up actions. It also compares feedback across sessions to see whether particular learning gaps are improving.

On Fridays, I hold a progress checkpoint where ChatGPT helps review recent lessons, highlight learning gaps, identify overdue actions, and suggest what to prioritise with each tutor. The biggest benefit is that I'm no longer just paying for tutoring and hoping it's working.”

items.title: Nvidia enters life without Jensen Huang
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,207 new readers. Two weeks ago, a NYT report tied Nvidia’s CEO to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Now, the man who turned a Denny’s-booth startup into the engine of the AI boom is out the door.

Jensen Huang has resigned after a 33-year run at Nvidia, leaving the world’s most important AI infrastructure company without its founder, and without a clear plan for what comes next.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia’s CEO

  • Rowan’s Corner: How I use AI to coach my calls

  • Build a shared tracker in Claude Sheets

  • Google joins the race for your face with AI glasses

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

NVIDIA

🚨 Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia’s CEO

Image source: Nvidia / The Rundown

The Rundown: Jensen Huang just resigned as Nvidia’s CEO and board member, effective immediately, after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset; CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO.

The details:

  • The exit came days after Huang admitted to infidelity following reports linking him to an alleged Chinese spy. The board backed him, saying it had “no reason to believe” national security or company secrets were compromised.

  • Pressure built after the NYT reported a second relationship with an Nvidia executive; Reuters reported a third with another employee after the resignation.

  • Kress, CFO since 2013, will hold both roles as the board looks for a replacement, with Trump pitching Tim Cook as the “only one man” who could take the job.

  • Nvidia closed down 4% Thursday after falling more than 14%, with earnings due Nov. 17 and House committee chairs seeking a closed-door briefing from Huang.

Why it matters: Over 33 years, Huang made Nvidia the company it is, taking it from gaming GPUs to the hardware behind modern AI. Under him, it stayed dominant even as rivals pushed their own chips. Whoever steps into his shoes will have to build on that and decide which of his fights to keep, from lighter AI regulation to chip sales to China.

TOGETHER WITH HUBSPOT

🧠 100+ ChatGPT prompts to revolutionize your workflow

Inside, you’ll find:

  • Quick crash course to master ChatGPT in under 30 minutes

Get your free copy.

ROWAN’S CORNER

📞 How I use AI to coach my calls

Screenshot via Forbes interview with Rowan

Rowan: After every high-stakes call, I let AI tear apart my performance. It started as a weird quirk several months ago, and it’s quietly become one of my most useful habits, so I figured it’s worth sharing.

The setup is simple. I record my meetings with Granola (you could use any meeting note taker), connect the transcripts to Claude, and instead of just pulling summaries and action items, I make it look backward at my own performance.

A few of the analyses I run:

  • My talk ratio on sales calls, flagged whenever it passes 50% (typically you want to talk less)

  • Every moment I dodged a hard topic or put off a decision I could’ve made on the spot

  • A commitment log of everything promised, including every “let me think about it,” which gets pushed into my to-do lists

  • An objection library of every pushback partners raised this year, with a stronger answer drafted for each

One quick tip if you try this is to ask for exact quotes, so Claude or ChatGPT puts your own words next to what you should’ve said.

And this works for way more than my calls. You could run the same workflow on recruiting calls, sales calls, leadership meetings, heck, even podcasts and interview recordings. If it’s recorded, it can coach you.

AI TRAINING

💻️ Build a shared tracker in Claude Sheets

The Rundown: Claude now builds its own spreadsheets, turning a description into a table and leaving the formulas in the cells, so you can check every number. In this guide, you’ll build a campaign tracker with status and budget, then share it for editing.

Step-by-step:

  1. Go to claude.ai/artifacts, click the green Sheets tile under Make something new, and describe the tracker: every column, dropdown values, and cells with formulas

  2. Click a total and read the formula bar. Then select the table, click Ask Claude, and ask it to point out any cell holding a typed number instead of a formula, since only formulas update when Spent changes

  3. Ask Claude to highlight tasks that are past their due date and not Done. Then paste your own tasks over the samples and have Claude delete the leftovers

  4. Click Share, invite a teammate with Can edit, and leave General access on Only you. On paid plans, people can edit cells but can’t ask Claude for changes

Pro tip: Before any big change, open Share, then the Export tab, and download an Excel copy. If an edit goes wrong, you still have the tracker as it was. For a bad build, Undo on the “Claude updated” notice takes the whole thing back.

Watch the full guide at The Rundown University →

PRESENTED BY INCOGNI

📞 That scam call wasn’t random

The Rundown: Scammers don’t guess your number — they buy it from data brokers selling your phone, home address, and relatives’ info online. That’s how a random call turns into phishing, impersonation, or worse. Incogni removes your data from these databases and keeps removing it automatically.

With Incogni working in the background, you can:

  • Keep phone numbers and addresses off broker databases

  • Reduce exposure to identity theft and impersonation

  • Let automated removals do the work continuously

Get 58% off with the code RUNDOWN.

GOOGLE

👓️ Google joins the race for your face with AI glasses

Image source: Google

The Rundown: Google opened pre-orders for its first Gemini-powered AI smart glasses, 18 months after announcing them at I/O 2025, with frames from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster starting at $395 in a direct challenge to Meta’s Ray-Bans.

The details:

  • Built with Samsung, the nine styles pack a 12MP camera, open-ear speakers, and up to nine hours of battery into 41-gram frames, with no display in the lenses.

  • Wearers can say “Hey Gemini” to ask about what they’re looking at, get Maps directions in their ear, play music, or translate speech live across 70+ languages.

  • Google says the glasses redact bystanders’ faces before Gemini sees them, show a light when recording, and stop recording if the light is covered; users can even control which apps access the camera and mic.

  • They go on sale Dec. 10 in the U.S. and South Korea and work with iPhones too, taking on Meta, which shipped 81% of AI glasses in the first half of the year.

Why it matters: Meta holds the crown in AI glasses, but privacy backlash over their cameras has dogged it, to the point it launched a camera-free model in September. With its new glasses and their added privacy features, Google is pitching itself as the safer pick, betting it can keep the camera and still earn the trust Meta has struggled to win.

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ A Rundown reader used AI to turn personal stories into published books

Today’s workflow comes from an anonymous Rundown reader:

“After retiring from medicine, I began writing personal stories and used ChatGPT to polish them for sharing. Over time, it helped me connect stories, identify larger themes, and explore new ideas. I bring my own stories, reflections, and questions, then work with ChatGPT through suggestions, revisions, and sometimes disagreements. I also use Claude and Gemini as independent reviewers to catch weaknesses or missed possibilities, while keeping all creative and editorial decisions my own.

This process has helped me publish books and create Creating Space, a collection of contemplative resources for individuals and groups. Each project sparks new questions and ideas. The biggest benefit hasn’t been saving time. At 73, I’ve begun to see myself as a creator, using AI to explore possibilities and bring my ideas to life while retaining responsibility for the work.”
